title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Leaflet Interactive Maps
Let’s start with a basic map of earthquakes near New Zealand. We can set the earthquakes to size by magnitude. I messed around with the math a little to get a size ratio that I liked.


Code
data(quakes)

quakes |>
  slice_sample(n = 300) |>
  leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    # set circle marker to size by magnitude
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    # make popup labels
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<strong>Magnitude:</strong> ", mag,
      "<br><strong>Depth:</strong> ", depth, " km"
    ),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.6
  )






Color the points by magnitude and add a legend:


Code
pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = quakes$mag
)

leaflet(quakes) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    color = ~pal(mag),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.7
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = ~mag,
    title = "Magnitude"
  )






Now let’s start playing around with the basemaps. You can find all of the possibilities on this website:
https://leaflet-extras.github.io/leaflet-providers/preview/


Code
library(leaflet)
library(dplyr)

data(quakes)

small <- quakes |> filter(mag < 5)
large <- quakes |> filter(mag >= 5)

leaflet() |>
  # Basemaps
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap", group = "Ocean") |>
  addProviderTiles("Stadia.StamenWatercolor", group = "Artsy") |>

  # Small earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = small,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = 3,
    color = "blue",
    group = "Smaller quakes",
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.5
  ) |>

  # Large earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = large,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag * 2,
    color = "red",
    group = "Larger quakes",
    stroke = TRUE,
    weight = 1
  ) |>

  # Layer control
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Satellite", "Ocean", "Artsy"),
    overlayGroups = c("Smaller quakes", "Larger quakes"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )

library(sf)
eji_data <- st_read("~/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/STAT 118/S2026/S2026_R_Proj/midterm/eji_sf.gpkg")

Code

  filter(STATE_NAME=="California") |>
  filter(!is.na(E_LIMENG), E_LIMENG <100)

pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",

)


eji_cali |>
leaflet() |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(E_LIMENG),

    popup = ~paste0(

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Plotly Interactive Plots
Plotly doesn’t change your analysis at all — it just changes how your results exist. It turns a static figure into something you could actually put on a website or share with someone to explore.
Let’s start simple. You make a plot in ggplot and then you feed it into plotly and it’s like magic.


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class,
                     text = paste("Model:", model))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s add more information to the pop-up:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = paste(
      "Model:", model,
      "<br>Class:", class,
      "<br>Displacement:", displ,
      "<br>Highway MPG:", hwy
    )),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s try it with the gapminder data.


Code
p <-  gapminder |> 
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(color="Continent") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 10)) +
  ggtitle("Year: 2007") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With facets:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~drv) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With a boxplot:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(class, hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is my first time doing this with a boxplot, and now this is the only way I’m making a boxplot ever again!
Let’s do it with a line!


Code
economics <- ggplot2::economics

p <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






WITH A DENSITY PLOT!


Code
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is AMAZING! Why am I only just learning this????

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Animation
This animation shows the gapminder dataset through time, with GDP per capita on the x-axis and Life expectancy on the y-axis. The points are colored by continent and sized by population (on a log scale).


Code
p <- ggplot(
  gapminder,
  aes(
    x = gdpPercap,
    y = lifeExp,
    group = country,
    color = continent,
    size = pop
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 10)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Year: {frame_time}",
    x = "GDP per capita",
    y = "Life expectancy",
    color = "Continent",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  transition_time(year)

animate(
  p,
  nframes = 60,
  fps = 4,
  width = 600,
  height = 400,
  renderer = gifski_renderer(),
  device = "ragg_png"
)


You may be able to tell by how many plots I made with the others and how few animations I have given you, that my heart isn’t really in animations. This single animation took about 50% of the time I spent making this. They can be a real pain. A good animation is absolute gold, but it is very hard to make a good animation.

section: Spatial Data - but not people data
text:
Spatial Data - but not people data


Code
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(cmocean)
library(ggthemes)
library(wesanderson)

volcano_df <- as.data.frame(volcano) |>
  mutate(y = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-y, names_to = "x", values_to = "elevation") |>
  mutate(x = as.numeric(gsub("V", "", x)))

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x, y, fill = elevation)) +
  geom_raster() + #not the way I choose to do this anymore, but workable for smaller data
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Topographic-style raster map")









Here is some code from my Data Science Across Disciplines class this last January looking at instrumented seal data from the Southern Ocean.
First, some data prep. You are not expected to understand this part.


Code
seal_data <- read_csv("~/Dropbox/!middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2026/R_code/MEOP_data_analysis/data/regional_data/par_seal_data.csv")
seal_data_surface <- seal_data |>
  filter(level==1)

raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif"))


#adjust seal data
seal_data_surface <- seal_data_surface |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

seal_data_mod <- seal_data |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

world <- map_data("world")


First a map with “raster” data.


Code
raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif")) 

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
   labs(fill="Depth (km)",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +
  ggtitle("Zoomed in on AAR/PAR, Bathymetry") +
  theme_tufte()









Code
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
  geom_point(data=seal_data_surface, 
             aes(x=lon_anti, y=lat, color=TEMP_ADJUSTED), 
             alpha=0.3, size=2) +
  scale_color_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  labs(fill="Depth (km)", color="Temp",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +
  ggtitle("Zoomed in on PAR, Bathymetry and Temperature") +
  theme_tufte()











Code
NPP_stack <- rast("~/Dropbox/!Research/Projects/PacAntRidge/data/NPP_raster_stack.nc")

invisible(capture.output({ #to suppress the #$^*@$ progress bar
NPP_stack[NPP_stack >100] = 100 #set max value
NPP_stack[NPP_stack <0] = NA #transform placeholder NA value (-99) to actual NA
}))

#my favorite palette from the wesanderson package
pal <- wes_palette("Zissou1", 100, type = "continuous")
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=NPP_stack[[15]]) + #index to show layer 15 only
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=pal, limits=c(0,100)) +
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) + #contour to show margins of mid ocean ridge
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) +
  theme_tufte() +
  ggtitle("NPP 2011-2012")









Code
#calculate the difference between the two years, by subtracting one from the other
diff_layer <- NPP_stack[[14]]-NPP_stack[[15]]

diff_layer[diff_layer > 75] = 75 #set max value
diff_layer[diff_layer < (-75)] = -75 #set min value


ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=diff_layer) + 
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="balance", limits=c(-75,75)) + #change to diverging palette
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) +
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) + #set this argument so that it doesn't add a border between the map and the axes
  theme_tufte() +
  ggtitle("NPP difference 2010-2011 minus 2011-2012")

text:

Github Website: Completed notes will be rendered and posted to the site
Github Code Repository: Files used for homeowrk assignments and .qmd versions of class notes, as well as template files for class notes will be availble here



Syllabus

Assignments: See the Syllabus and Schedule for more details, but briefly, you will have 2 Homework Assignments per week, a Midterm Project, and a Final Project
Grade Allocation: Homework is 40% of your grade, Midterm Project is 25% and Final Project is 35%
Late Policy: See Syllabus for details



Thoughts on AI

Assignment prompts: You will be prompted at the end of your Homework Assignments to tell me whether you used AI, how you used it, and how you think it helped or hindered your learning
Thinking about what it gives you and what it takes away: I am not here to police your use of AI, but I do think it requires important consideration of how it impacts your learning (either positively or negatively)



Download Notes Template
These will always be linked on the Schedule (on the Canvas Site) before each class. You should download these at the beginning of class so that you will be better able to code along with me in class.


Directory structure
The directory structure outlined below is intended to prevent a number of headaches in how Quarto references files automatically. Please make sure that your files and folders are structured like this.
📁 STAT118/
   ├── class-notes.qmd
   ├── homework-01.qmd
   ├── homework-02.qmd
   ├── 📁 data/
   └── 📁 images/


R and Rstudio

What is the difference?
R is the engine and RStudio is the car.


What do the different windows do?
The Source window is where you will create and edit your Quarto documents, and write your code. This window should be in the top left pane.
The Console window is where the code is run. This window should be in the top right pane.
The Environment window will show you the objects and other things that you have created and defined in your code. this should be on the bottom left.
The window on the lower right should include Files, Plots, Packages, Help, and Viewer (it’s ok if there are additional tabs). This is where you can look for help documentation on the different functions available through R and additional R packages. This is also where figures and rendered files should pop up.



Settings

Rearrange panes
If your panes are not in the configuration outlined above, please change them using the instructions below.
Go to:
Tools → Global Options → Pane Layout


Change theme
If you want to change how your RStudio appears.
We decided that I could continue to use my dark theme. Yay!
Go to:
Tools → Global Options → Appearance


Change Downloads Permission
Please take a minute to change your downloads permissions for the browser that you use. This will make it easier for you to direct downloads to the correct folder and not have to go hunting for things that got sent to weird places.
Google Chrome:

Go to the three-dot menu (top-right corner) → Settings.
Scroll down and click Downloads.
Toggle on “Ask where to save each file before downloading.”

Firefox:

Click the three-line menu (top-right corner) → Settings.
In the General section, under Files and Applications, select: “Always ask you where to save files.”

Safari (Mac):

Go to Safari > Preferences > General.
Under File download location, select: “Ask for each download.”




Quarto

Source vs. Visual


Markdown Syntax

Bold and Italics
You make bold text by placing two * before and after the text you wish to bold: **make this text bold**
make this text bold
You make italics text by placing one * before and after the text you wish to appear in italics: *make this text italics*
make this text italics
You make bold and italics text by placing three * before and after the text you wish to appear in bold and italics: ***make this text bold and italics***
make this text bold and italics


Lists
To make a list put a - before each item on the list.
a list

-   one thing
-   second thing
-   third thing

The result will look like this:
a list

one thing
second thing
third thing

Always make sure to include an empty line before the first item on the list, otherwise it will not render properly.


Hyperlink
To add a hyperlink use this syntax:
[words here](link here)
The text should look like this:
[this is a link to the class website](https://cschine.github.io/my_class_website/courses/STAT118/)
The result will look like this:
this is a link to the class website


Images
To add an image, use this syntax:
![caption](image)
The text should look something like this:
![this is an image](images/NBP_midnight_sun.jpeg)
And the result will look like this:



this is an image





Using R in Quarto
R code chunks
Use the green +C buttom in the toolbar to add a code chunk
Create an object like this:

aardvark <- 17

yeti <- 23

You can do basic arithmetic with named objects using the standard operators:



Operator
Description




+
Addition


-
Subtraction


*
Multiplication


/
Division


^ or **
Exponentiation



Like this:

aardvark*yeti

[1] 391

aardvark/yeti

[1] 0.7391304

chalk <- aardvark*yeti

chalk

[1] 391


To comment code use the # at the beginning of the line and write a description of what the code should be doing, or a note to yourself, or whatever you want. Like this:

# multiply aardvark and yeti
aardvark*yeti

[1] 391

# divide aardvark by yeti
aardvark/yeti

[1] 0.7391304

# assign chalk a value of aardvark multiplied by yeti
chalk <- aardvark*yeti

# call chalk up
chalk

[1] 391




Render
Now it is time to Render your Quarto (.qmd) doc into a .html file (which is the format in which you will be submitting all of your assignments). To do this press the  Render button, which should be visible in the toolbar at the top of your Source Pane (the pane in which you are editing your Quarto document).
If your quarto doc does not render correctly, errors can be found in the Background Jobs tab in the Console Pane. This can be very useful and sometimes very confusing.



Assignments
Assignments will be linked on the Schedule on Canvas. If you are having any difficulty with your assignment please come to office hours sooner rather than later so that we can get things figured out.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
For this course, you will need to install both R and RStudio on your computer.

R is the programming language that runs your code.
RStudio is the program we will use to write and run R code.

Install R first, then install RStudio.

1. Install R
Go to the R Project download page.

Mac

Click Download R for macOS.
Download the appropriate installer for your Mac.
Open the downloaded .pkg file and follow the installation instructions.







Tip



If you are unsure which R version you need, click on the Apple in the upper lefthand corner of your desktop and select “About This Mac”, this will contain information both about the chip in your Mac (Intel or M) and the OS that you are running which will allow you to select the correct version of R.




Windows

Click Download R for Windows.
Click install R for the first time.
Click Download R-4.6.1 for Windows (the exact R version number may have changed).
Open the downloaded installer and accept the default installation options.




2. Install RStudio Desktop
Go to the RStudio Desktop download page.

Download the free version of RStudio Desktop for your operating system.
Open the installer.
Follow the installation instructions.



3. Make sure everything works
Open RStudio.



Credit: moderndive


If the installation was successful, you should see the RStudio interface with a Console pane containing some text about your version of R and a > prompt.
At the > prompt, type:

2 + 2

If R responds with:
[1] 4
you’re ready for class!
If you are stumped by 3. Don’t worry about it. If you didn’t get any errors during installation and can open the program ok, then you should be good to go.

3️⃣ Render and Preview
Click the Render button () at the top-right of your RStudio editor window.
Tada! You now have created a .html file!
The file has been created in the same folder as your .qmd file: 
When you render, a preview of the document will show up!






Tip



By default, the preview of .html will pop up in your web browser. This is totally okay. In fact, I tend to prefer this approach when I’m working at a computer station with multiple monitors.
However, you may prefer to have the .html preview in your viewer pane right within RStudio. This is what I prefer when I’m just working on just my laptop.
Click on the “gear button”  and select “Preview in Viewer Pane”


The preview will update whenever you re-render the document.

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
A package is a bundle of tools that someone has written and shared to help you do specific kinds of work in R.
It usually contains:

Functions (the main thing you use)
Documentation (help files)
Sometimes example datasets

A package is like installing an “app” for R. Base R is what comes pre-installed and Packages are extra apps you download when you need new features



A function is a named command that does a specific job.
You give it inputs → it does something → it gives you an output.
It is like a button on a calculator. You press “mean” → it computes the mean.

Installing a package
You can install a package by selecting the packages tab your console pane where you have Files, Plots, Packages, etc. Then click on the install icon at the top left. Start typing in the package you want to install. It will give you some autofill options, you can type the whole thing in or select it from the autofill options. Then click on ‘Install’.
You can also run a simple line of code (which you can see in your R Console is what all the button clicking in the previous paragraph does).

# package name must be in quotes
#install.packages("tidyverse")

# after you have installed the package you do not need to install it again

You only run the install.packages() function for a given package one time and then once the package is installed you should not run this line of code again. Either comment it out or delete it. Now you have a copy of the package saved on your computer.

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
Loading packages
Once a package is installed you need to load it. This makes the package available in your current R session.
I highly recommend creating a setup code chunk at the beginning of each of your Quarto documents where you load in all of the packages that you will need. If you load an additional package later in the document, circle back around and add it to your setup chunk.

#set this to suppress a warning or message when you run a chunk
#| warning: FALSE 
#| message: FALSE

library(tidyverse)

Today we are specifically going to be talking about the package dplyr which is useful to manipulating data sets.

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
distinct()
We can use distinct to get more information from the can_lang dataset. Such as the number of different language categories in the dataset.

# ?distinct() to look at the help documentation
# distinct() also to get list of languages can filter by

# using distinct without the pipe
distinct(select(can_lang, category))

# A tibble: 3 × 1
  category                               
  <chr>                                  
1 Aboriginal languages                   
2 Non-Official & Non-Aboriginal languages
3 Official languages                     

# using distinct with pipe
can_lang |>
  select(category) |>
  distinct()

# A tibble: 3 × 1
  category                               
  <chr>                                  
1 Aboriginal languages                   
2 Non-Official & Non-Aboriginal languages
3 Official languages

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
filter()
We can use the filter function to extract rows from the data that match a certain condition or set of conditions.
We define the condition with a logical expression using the logical operators are given below:



Operator
Description




<
Less than


>
Greater than


<=
Less than or equal to


>=
Greater than or equal to


==
Equal to


!=
Not equal to


!x
Not x


x | y
x OR y


x & y
x AND y



For example, we may be interested in only looking at only the languages in this dataset that are Aboriginal languages.

# ?filter() for help documentation
# wants data and an expression that returns a logical value


# filter for only Aboriginal languages using pipe

can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages")

# filter and then pipe into count() to get number of Aboriginal languages

can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages") |>
  count()

  <int>
1    67


Oftentimes, we want to take our subset and give it a new name. This takes our subset and assigns it to a new dataset called aboriginal_lang.

# define new object with only aboriginal languages

aboriginal_lang <- can_lang |>
  filter(category == "Aboriginal languages")

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
arrange()
The arrange function allows us to order the rows of the data frame by the values of a particular column.
For example, arrange all the aboriginal languages in canada by from most to least spoken as mother tongue.

# filter for Aboriginal languages category then arrange (desc)

# ascending arrangement by mother_tongue

can_lang |>
  filter(category=="Aboriginal languages") |>
  arrange(mother_tongue)

# A tibble: 67 × 6
   category          language mother_tongue most_at_home most_at_work lang_known
   <chr>             <chr>            <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
 1 Aboriginal langu… Wakasha…            10            0            0         25
 2 Aboriginal langu… Iroquoi…            35            5            0        115
 3 Aboriginal langu… Squamish            40            5           10        285
 4 Aboriginal langu… Algonqu…            45           10            0        120
 5 Aboriginal langu… Cayuga              45           10           10        125
 6 Aboriginal langu… Souther…            45           15            0         40
 7 Aboriginal langu… Athabas…            50           10            0         85
 8 Aboriginal langu… Siouan …            55           20            0        140
 9 Aboriginal langu… Oneida              60           15            0        185
10 Aboriginal langu… Souther…            70            5            0        145
# ℹ 57 more rows

can_lang |>
  filter(category=="Aboriginal languages") |>
  arrange(desc(mother_tongue))

title: Wrangling Basics
text:
mutate()
mutate() creates new columns that are functions of existing variables.
For example, if I want to create a new column called mother_tongue_K which represents the number of people who speak the language their mother tongue in thousands. You may want to save this new dataset over top of the original dataset so you could use this new column in the future.

# make a column of all 5


# mutate on column of mother_tongue/1000


# do the same thing as above but add a column of 1000 and then do the math with the columns


# add multiple columns together

This can be useful for unit conversions. It also be useful for making new calculations based on existing data (for example, price and number of square feet could be used to calculate price per square foot).
